title: Social Communication
summary: Communication is a process of interaction with people and the environment in which information, ideas and attitudes are transmitted, to bring about a change in behaviour; it is a tool for controlling and motivating people. Five key elements: (i) a two-way process between a sender and a receiver (individual or group level); (ii) a message (information, directive, idea, feeling or opinion); (iii) commonness of understanding (culture, language, environment; words, idioms, gestures, proverbs); (iv) modifying the behaviour of others (people run out when told of fire); (v) a method of giving information (words, gestures, expressions).

Verbal communication uses words, oral or written (conversation, speeches, letters, newspapers, telephone); a person spends 10–11 hours a day in reading, speaking, writing or listening. Non-verbal communication or body language accounts for more than 70 per cent of communication while words are about 10 per cent (another estimate gives 7–35 per cent for spoken language). It includes gestures, eye contact, facial expressions, posture, body orientation and distance; it creates impressions, reinforces what is said, expresses emotions and attitudes, conveys power, affection, dominance and respect, regulates interaction and allows self-presentation; it is influenced by culture. Four channels: kinesics (body language), gaze (eye contact), proxemics (use of social distance: intimate 0–18 inches, personal 18 inches–4 feet, social 4–12 feet, public beyond 12 feet) and haptics (touch; North Americans and North Europeans touch less, Asians, Mediterranean and Middle Eastern people more). Direct eye contact shows confidence, looking down shows respect or guilt, a single raised eyebrow doubt and both raised admiration; erect, slightly forward posture shows approachability; a smile shows happiness and friendliness.

Barriers: people may change facts to please the boss; selective perception based on needs, motivation and experience; projection of interests in decoding; information overload (limited processing capacity); emotions (sad, angry, excited) causing missing information; different meanings of words by age, gender and culture. Features of effective communication: common frame of reference, mutual interest, common language and common environment (nationality, status, culture, age group, profession). Tips for verbal communication: improve language by reading and listening, work on voice modulation and pronunciation, think before speaking, do not speak too fast or loudly, learn culturally sensitive words. Body language tips: keep appropriate distance (culture, gender, authority), touch only if necessary, eye contact in an interview, look presentable and confident. Advertisers combine words, images, music and famous people (jingles).
## Non-verbal communication in the Indian context

Couples are not expected to show intimacy in public or in front of family; sliding a hand over the wrist (bangle gesture) to a man questions his manhood; handshakes are common between men or between women and avoided between a man and a woman, though common in corporate Delhi and Mumbai. India has a high power-distance index: hierarchy, authority and age shape distance and eye contact; the superior may look directly while the subordinate stands with downcast eyes at a reasonable distance (employer–employee, father–son, daughter-in-law and husband's elders); women often do not hold eye contact with husband's male relatives and may cover the head with a veil. Personal space is 1.5–2 metres, but there is little distance with family and close friends; each member is bid goodbye individually; youngsters touch the feet of elders.

Media is the technological means of sending information and opinions to a large audience (newspapers, radio, television, Internet). Positive influences: educates and improves academic performance, distributes news, promotes literacy and health (vaccination, polio, AIDS), transmits social and cultural values, informs about government policy, maintains democracy and brings social integration. Negative: misuse by spreading wrong information, rumours and propaganda that lead to violence, prejudice and communal hatred; violation of privacy; vulgar and obscene material; influence on children about fashion, body image and lifestyle. Media must maintain ethics: objective, balanced and accurate information, avoid inciting crime, violence and hatred, and work for community building and national integration.

Sender and receiver share a base such as culture, language and environment, making words, idioms and gestures meaningful to both.
It makes up most of communication, reinforces words, expresses emotions and attitudes and regulates interaction.
The use of social distance between people: intimate, personal, social and public space.
A situation in which too much information exceeds a person's limited capacity, so some is ignored or forgotten.

sa: Explain the key elements of communication.
Two-way sender–receiver process, a message, commonness of understanding, modification of the receiver's behaviour and a method of giving information (words or gestures).
Describe the functions of non-verbal communication.
It creates impressions beyond words, reinforces speech, expresses emotions and attitudes, conveys power, affection, respect, regulates interaction and allows self-presentation; it is culture-bound.
Describe the barriers to effective communication.
Distortion of facts to please others, selective perception, projection in decoding, information overload, emotional states and differing meanings of words by age, gender and culture.
Describe the features of effective communication.
Common frame of reference, mutual interest, common language and common environment ensure minimum misunderstanding.
Give tips for improving verbal and body language.

Read and listen to improve language, modulate voice, think before speaking, avoid speaking fast or loudly; keep appropriate distance, touch only if needed, keep eye contact in interviews and look confident.
Describe the negative impacts of media.
Spread of wrong news, rumours and propaganda leading to violence and prejudice, invasion of privacy, vulgar material and unhealthy influence on children's body image and lifestyle.
la: Define communication and discuss its five elements with examples.

Communication is interaction to transmit information and bring behaviour change. Elements: two-way process (teacher to students), message (idea or feeling), commonness of understanding (language, culture), behaviour change (running out when told of a fire) and a method (words or gestures).
Discuss verbal and non-verbal communication and their importance.

Verbal uses spoken or written words (10–11 hours daily). Non-verbal (more than 70 per cent) uses kinesics, gaze, proxemics (four distance zones) and haptics; eye contact, posture and smile convey meaning. It supports words, expresses emotion, regulates interaction and varies with culture.
Explain the barriers and the features of effective communication.

Barriers: distortion, selective perception, projection, overload, emotions and differing word meanings. Effective communication needs a common frame of reference, mutual interest, common language and common environment, plus tips: voice modulation, thinking before speaking, appropriate distance and culturally sensitive signs.
Discuss non-verbal communication in the Indian context and the role of media.

In India no public intimacy between couples, bangle gesture, handshakes mainly same-sex, a high power-distance (downcast eyes before superiors, veils, touching feet), personal space of 1.5–2 metres. Media informs, educates and integrates but can spread rumours, hatred and obscenity; it must follow ethics and promote national integration.
